item.title: Ollama Tool Calls: Object vs String Arguments on Two API Surfaces
item.description: Same prompt, same qwen3:0.6b call: /api/chat returns arguments as an object, /v1/chat/completions as a JSON string, and replaying either history returns HTTP 400. The two error strings, a tested normaliser, and the streaming shape that looks hung.
item.content:encoded:
A coding agent works for an afternoon against Ollama’s native /api/chat. Then someone points the OpenAI SDK at http://localhost:11434/v1 to reuse an existing client, or a library switches endpoints underneath the agent. The first turn still works. The second turn is where the run dies, in one of two ways that look unrelated:

  • the executor calls args["path"] and gets TypeError: string indices must be integers, not 'str', because the arguments arrived as a JSON string;
  • or the client stores the native assistant message, sends it back to /v1/chat/completions, and gets HTTP 400 before a single token is generated.

Both failures have the same cause: the two surfaces of the same server encode a tool call in incompatible ways. On Ollama 0.20.3, non-streaming, with qwen3:0.6b, POST /api/chat returned function.arguments as a JSON object. POST /v1/chat/completions, same model, same prompt, same tools array, returned the same call with function.arguments as a JSON string. Replaying either assistant message into the other endpoint was rejected with 400, each with its own parse error.

That is the whole finding, and it is a client problem rather than a server defect: each endpoint returns a well-formed call in its own encoding. The rest of this article is the measured evidence, the two error strings to grep for, a normaliser that survives both shapes, and the streaming behaviour that makes a correct client look hung.

What each specification actually says

Neither encoding is an accident. Ollama’s own API specification types tool-call arguments as an object: the ToolCall.function schema in docs.ollama.com/openapi.yaml declares

arguments:
  type: object
  description: JSON object of arguments to pass to the function

The OpenAI chat-completions schema types the same field as a string, and warns that the string is not guaranteed to be valid JSON. In the OpenAI OpenAPI specification:

arguments:
  type: string
  description: The arguments to call the function with, as generated by the model
    in JSON format.

So a client that moves between the two surfaces is not decoding the same type twice; it is decoding an object on one side and a serialised object on the other. Ollama’s OpenAI-compatibility page is explicit that the /v1 layer is partial — “Ollama supports a subset of the OpenAI API” — which is consistent with what follows. The string return on /v1 matches the OpenAI schema; the object return on /api/chat matches Ollama’s. A library that assumes one shape is correct only on the surface it was written for.

This is also the specific place where our own guide to Ollama’s two API surfaces overstates parity. Its sentence “Both approaches produce identical inference results” holds for plain text and does not hold for tool calls, as the measurement below shows. For a vanished or retyped call rather than an encoding mismatch, see the history-corruption cases; those are server-side parser and renderer defects, and they are a different failure. If you want the mechanism behind function calling first, the tool-use explainer covers it, and the tool-definition token cost piece covers what the same request spends before generation starts.

The measurement: one host, one model, one prompt

One read_file tool (path: string, max_bytes: integer, both required), one user message — “Read the file src/app.py and report the first 2000 bytes.” — sent to both endpoints of the same local server, temperature 0, native request with think: false. Environment: Ollama 0.20.3, qwen3:0.6b digest 7df6b6e09427 (Q4_K_M), 2 vCPU / 11 GB, localhost only, no credentials and no external network. Measured 2026-11-15; the two specification excerpts above were reopened on 2026-11-25 and are dated separately from the probe.

POST /api/chat POST /v1/chat/completions
HTTP status 200 200
tool-call keys id, function (index, name, arguments) id, index, type, function
function.arguments object → Python dict JSON string → Python str
argument value {"path": "src/app.py", "max_bytes": 2000} "{\"path\":\"src/app.py\",\"max_bytes\":2000}"
tool-call id call_3nn9ernp call_im2sam5h
assistant message keys role, content, tool_calls role, content, reasoning, tool_calls
stop field done_reason: "stop" finish_reason: "tool_calls"
token counts prompt_eval_count 175, eval_count 32 usage 169 / 134 / 303
wall clock (includes load) 36.9 s 74.1 s

The raw bodies are published: /api/chat request, /api/chat response, /v1 request, /v1 response.

Two details in that table matter more than they look. The native response reports done_reason: "stop" on a turn that contains a tool call, while the compatible response reports finish_reason: "tool_calls". A client that treats stop as “the model finished talking” and never inspects tool_calls will silently discard a perfectly good call on the native surface. And the /v1 message carries a reasoning field with the model’s thinking text, which the native message from this think: false request does not carry.

Wall-clock numbers are load-inclusive observations from one 2 vCPU host, not a benchmark; this article makes no throughput claim.

Two client bugs, one wire difference

The shapes fail differently in client code, which is why the same root cause produces unrelated-looking tracebacks.

Decoding an OpenAI-shaped call with json.loads works; decoding a native call that way raises TypeError: the JSON object must be str, bytes or bytearray, not dict. Consuming a native call with args["path"] works; consuming an OpenAI-shaped call that way raises TypeError: string indices must be integers, not 'str', quoted here from the interpreter rather than paraphrased — the string is indexed by "path", which Python rejects because string indices must be integers. Libraries that parse arguments in exactly one place get one of these, and libraries that parse in two places get the other on the second turn.

The history side is worse, because it is the server rejecting the request rather than the client misreading a value. Both directions were measured, and both returned 400 immediately — before generation, so 0.0 s wall:

native assistant turn -> POST /v1/chat/completions
400 {"error":{"message":"json: cannot unmarshal object into Go struct field .messages.tool_calls.function.arguments of type string","type":"invalid_request_error","param":null,"code":null}}

openai assistant turn -> POST /api/chat
400 {"error":"Value looks like object, but can't find closing '}' symbol"}

Transcripts: native history replayed into /v1 and OpenAI history replayed into /api/chat. Both files contain the exact request that was sent, so you can replay them against your own server.

Read those messages as version-scoped fingerprints rather than API contracts. The first is a Go encoding/json error naming .messages.tool_calls.function.arguments and the expected type string; the second is Ollama’s own message parser failing to read a string that looks like an object. The durable behaviour to test for is the 400 on cross-endpoint replay; the exact strings may change between releases. If a future version coerces the type instead of rejecting it, the failure disappears and this section becomes historical.

The practical consequence is a rule about what to store between turns. Keep tool calls in the encoding of the endpoint you are about to call, or keep a neutral representation and serialise at the edge. Do not pass the native assistant message straight into an OpenAI-compatible client’s history, and do not pass the OpenAI-shaped one back to /api/chat. The tool-call id is no help either. Each response generated its own call, and the two ids (call_3nn9ernp natively, call_im2sam5h on /v1) are unrelated strings, so a proxy that rewrites ids across surfaces (the layer LiteLLM-style translation deals with) still has to fix the argument type.

A normaliser that survives both shapes

The adapter below is the minimum that handles what was actually observed: object arguments, string arguments, one nested wrapper (a model occasionally emits {"arguments": "{...}"}), and the empty case where the turn carries no call at all. It validates the decoded mapping against the schema that was sent, so a string that decodes to a list or a missing required key fails loudly instead of reaching the executor.

def normalise_tool_call(message, schema):
    calls = message.get("tool_calls") or []
    if len(calls) != 1:
        raise ToolCallShapeError("expected exactly 1 tool call, found %d" % len(calls))
    fn = calls[0].get("function") or {}
    args = fn.get("arguments")
    if isinstance(args, str):
        args = json.loads(args)          # OpenAI-compatible surface
    elif isinstance(args, dict):
        args = dict(args)                # native surface
    else:
        raise ToolCallShapeError("arguments is %s" % type(args).__name__)
    if "arguments" in args and len(args) <= 2:   # model-invented wrapper
        args = json.loads(args["arguments"]) if isinstance(args["arguments"], str) else args["arguments"]
    missing = [k for k in schema.get("required", []) if k not in args]
    if missing:
        raise ToolCallShapeError("missing required argument(s): %s" % ", ".join(missing))
    return fn.get("name"), args

The listing above is a condensed variant of the published file, not a verbatim excerpt: the json import, the ToolCallShapeError class and the per-property type checks are omitted for space, and the full file is normalise_tool_call.py, with per-property type validation. Its --selftest runs four cases — the two measured shapes plus the nested wrapper and the empty turn — using the exact argument objects returned by this run. Those four checks passed on Python 3.12.3 at 2026-11-25T12:54:29Z; the captured run is normalise_selftest_output.txt. That is a local fixture check of the adapter, not a model measurement: no model was called to produce it.

Streaming: 2 chunks versus 100, and why a correct client looks hung

Streaming was measured on the same prompt. The native surface produced 2 NDJSON chunks in 5.1 s, with the complete call inside the message object of the first chunk: tool_calls_per_chunk was [1, 0], no content and no thinking text.

The OpenAI-compatible surface produced 100 SSE chunks in 42.9 s. Of those, 98 carried delta.reasoning (394 characters in total), none carried delta.content, and exactly one carried the tool call — whole, with the arguments string not fragmented across deltas. The run’s usage block was absent from the stream. Raw chunk dumps: native and /v1.

A client written against the native stream expects the first chunk to be the answer. On the compatible stream it receives dozens of chunks whose content is empty and whose only payload is reasoning text, so its idle timer, its “first token” log line and its progress bar all behave as though the server were stuck — while the server is generating normally. The extra time is a property of this probe’s request rather than a claim about the endpoint: the native call here carried think: false, while the /v1/chat/completions request carried no thinking control at all and still came back with 394 reasoning characters in the stream and a reasoning field in the non-streamed message, which is why the same call took 42.9 s streamed and 74.1 s non-streamed against 5.1 s and 36.9 s natively. Ollama’s compatibility page documents reasoning_effort and reasoning.effort as thinking control on that surface, with "none" requesting false for boolean-only models; this run sent neither field, so it tested neither and says nothing about whether they would suppress the reasoning text on 0.20.3.

Two cautions before copying the usual SSE advice. First, this run did not observe fragmented arguments: the whole call arrived in one delta, so the article does not claim fragmentation happens on this model. A robust client should still assemble fragments, because that is the documented OpenAI behaviour, but this measurement is not evidence that it occurs here. Second, chunk counts, reasoning volume and wall times are this run’s observations, not constants; only the argument type, the status codes and the error bodies were stable enough to treat as findings.

What this is not

  • Not an Ollama bug. Both endpoints returned a correct, self-consistent call, and the compatibility layer is documented as a subset. The mismatch lives in clients that assume one encoding.
  • Not a statement about hosted OpenAI. No request was sent to api.openai.com; the OpenAI schema is cited only because the /v1 layer imitates it.
  • Not generalisable beyond this setup. One version (0.20.3), one model (qwen3:0.6b, digest 7df6b6e09427), one prompt, one host. Another model may serialise differently or emit no call at all.
  • Not a performance result. Wall-clock times include model load and are reported as observations from a 2 vCPU machine.

Reproduce it against your own server

Everything needed to re-run the probe and diff your server version is published with this page. shape_probe.py is standard-library Python: it posts to /api/chat with think: false, posts the same messages and tools to /v1/chat/completions, streams both, replays each assistant turn into the opposite endpoint, and writes one JSON file per step. METHOD.md records the environment and the determinism caveats, and 00_summary.json is the machine-readable summary behind every table cell above.

Run it as python3 shape_probe.py <out_dir> against a local Ollama with qwen3:0.6b pulled. It contacts localhost only — no credentials, no paid API, no external network — and takes roughly two to three minutes on 2 vCPU, most of it in the /v1 reasoning tokens. If your run returns string arguments on both endpoints, or accepts cross-endpoint replay, that is a real result too: name your version and model, because the behaviour is version-scoped and your negative result supersedes this one for your deployment.

The fix in your own code is small and does not need a server change: normalise the arguments at the boundary, keep history in the encoding of the endpoint you will call next, and do not read done_reason: "stop" as proof that nothing was called.

item.title: Ollama Tool Calls: Same Seed, Different Bytes
item.description: 13 replays of one fixed tool-calling request on Ollama 0.20.3 with qwen3:0.6b at seed 42: all 13 calls were semantically identical, but only 11 were byte-identical, and both flips happened at temperature 0.0. Includes the probe, the raw per-call JSONL and a normalise-then-hash helper.
item.content:encoded:
A team re-runs its agent eval after a one-line prompt change and the pass rate moves five points. They revert the prompt; the number does not come back. They blame the harness, then the model vendor, and eventually pin temperature=0 and seed=42 everywhere — and the number still moves. Nobody in that loop can answer the question that comes before all of it: at the sampling settings the harness already uses, is the emitted tool call even the same object twice?

Three different properties get conflated in that question. Semantic agreement is the same tool name with the same argument values, which is all an eval should assert on. Byte identity is the same argument text, including key order and numeric formatting, which is what a golden-file or snapshot test actually asserts on. Prompt-shape dependence is the fact that the same question asked as turn one and as turn four arrives with different history and different prefill, so a flip measured in one shape says nothing about the other.

This page answers four questions with a measurement rather than an argument: how often a pinned call repeats semantically and how often byte-for-byte; whether those two rates differ and in which direction; whether adding one history turn or padding the prompt changes either; and what a harness should therefore assert. The sample is small and is stated up front so nothing below has to be discounted later: 13 calls across four prompt shapes, one model, one host, seed 42, zero errors. All 13 were semantically identical. Eleven of 13 were byte-identical, and both of the byte flips happened at temperature=0.0. The N=20-per-condition matrix in the original plan was not run — the attempt budget does not hold 20–40 minutes of wall time on the host — so the numbers below are counts with denominators, not rates, and the difference matters.

What the vendors actually promise

Ollama’s API documentation offers the seed as the route to repeatability: “For reproducible outputs, set seed to a number” (github.com/ollama/ollama/blob/main/docs/api.md). Its Modelfile reference states the promise more directly — setting seed to a specific number “will make the model generate the same text for the same prompt” (docs/modelfile.mdx). vLLM frames the same property at the sampling layer, and goes further about temperature: “In V1, the seed parameter defaults to 0 which sets the random state for each worker, so the results will remain consistent for each vLLM run even if temperature > 0” — while also opening its page with “vLLM does not guarantee the reproducibility of the results by default, for the sake of performance” (docs.vllm.ai reproducibility).

Both promises are about the same kind of object: generated text, or the random state that produces it. The thing an agent harness asserts on is a different kind of object. tool_calls[0].function.arguments is a structured value that the server serialises back to JSON, and a JSON object is, per RFC 8259, “an unordered collection of zero or more name/value pairs” (rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8259.txt). Two serialisations of the same arguments can therefore differ in member order while denoting the same value. None of the three vendor pages above says anything about member order in a structured argument payload, and none of them measures it. A harness that treats the serialised arguments as a string inherits a property that its vendor documentation never claimed to control.

What was measured, and what it cannot tell you

The fixture is one fixed coding-agent request: a single tool stat_path with path (string), mode (enum stat|read|hash) and max_bytes (integer), and the instruction “Check whether docs/config.md exists and get its hash. Use the tool.” Every response was recorded verbatim; no expected output was written by hand. The probe posted to http://127.0.0.1:11434/api/chat with stream=false, think=false, num_predict=80, num_ctx=4096 and seed=42, and recorded per call the raw arguments value, the deserialised object, its key order, and two digests: sha256(json.dumps(args)) for the byte form and sha256(json.dumps(args, sort_keys=True)) for the semantic form.

The server was Ollama 0.20.3 on a CPU-only Linux host (2 vCPU, 11 GB RAM, no GPU). The model was qwen3:0.6b, digest 7df6b6e09427a769808717c0a93cadc4ae99ed4eb8bf5ca557c90846becea435, Q4_K_M, 751.63M parameters as reported by the server. qwen2.5:0.5b was installed and identified but not measured, so nothing here is a two-model claim. The four conditions and their sample sizes are in the table below; the exact environment, request body and the deviations from the original plan are in METHOD.md.

Condition Shape Temp N Semantic distinct Byte distinct Byte identical Key orders observed prompt_eval_count
S1 single turn 0.0 4 1 1 4/4 (path,mode)×4 197
S2 one prior turn (user, assistant tool_call, tool result) 0.0 3 1 2 2/3 (mode,path)×2, (path,mode)×1 268
S3 ~1,200-token repository listing prefix (1,420 total prompt tokens) 0.0 3 1 2 2/3 (path,mode)×2, (mode,path)×1 1,420
S4 single turn 0.7 3 1 1 3/3 (path,mode)×3 197

Three caveats belong next to that table rather than after it. The host was shared with a concurrent stage workload for the entire window, so wall time was recorded but is not interpretable and no latency or throughput claim is made. The design was round-robin rather than condition-by-condition, because a sequential loop would have spent the whole budget on S1 when each long-prompt call took 87–116 seconds. And the digests score the arguments object as the /api/chat response serialises it — this run cannot separate a model-side token-order difference from a server-side parse-and-reserialise step, and does not assert which it was.

Result: 13/13 semantic, 11/13 byte

Every one of the 13 calls emitted exactly one tool call, named stat_path, with path=docs/config.md, mode=hash and no max_bytes. Argument values never drifted, no required argument went missing, and no extra field appeared. Under sorted-key comparison the 13 calls collapse to a single digest; replayed through the normaliser in the last section, all 13 records produce one distinct semantic digest.

Byte identity is the part that did not hold. In S2 and S3, one call out of three carried the same two members in the opposite order from its two siblings. The flip is the whole finding, so it is worth seeing in full:

{"path": "docs/config.md", "mode": "hash"}
{"mode": "hash", "path": "docs/config.md"}

That is a difference a consumer of the call cannot observe — json.loads produces an equal dict either way — and a difference a text diff observes immediately. In this sample it appeared in the two conditions whose prompt was not the minimal one, and it did not appear at temperature=0.7.

Which is exactly where the result has to be handled carefully. The most tempting sentence to write here is “temperature does not matter”, and it is not supported. With N=3–4 there is no power to order conditions by flip probability; temperature and prompt shape are confounded with which condition happened to catch a flip; and 3/3 stability at temperature=0.7 is not evidence that 0.7 is safer. The defensible claim is narrower and still useful: in this sample, pinning temperature=0 was not sufficient for byte identity, so a harness that attributes a moved pass rate to its prompt has at least one other candidate cause it has not eliminated.

Why a golden-file test is the wrong assertion

A snapshot test that stores json.dumps(arguments) and compares strings is asserting on member order. JSON defines that order as carrying no meaning, so the assertion is stricter than the contract the data is published under. The failure modes that follow are ordinary and expensive:

  • Snapshot churn for no reason. A stored call expires because the same value came back in a different order. Someone re-records the snapshot; the test goes green; nobody learns anything.
  • Retry accounting that hides the real difference. If a harness retries on snapshot mismatch, a flip costs an extra call and the recorded pass rate now depends on retry policy — a separate and much better-documented hazard (agent-tool-retry-duplicate-side-effects-2026).
  • A pass rate that moves for reasons unrelated to the change under test. This is the opening scene. The flip is not proof that it explains a five-point move — 13 calls cannot support that — but it is a mechanism that produces exactly that symptom while every input is held fixed.

Two adjacent failures are worth separating out, because both look like this and neither is. An agent that repeats a failing action because its loop has no state guard is a control-flow bug, not sampling variance (deterministic-agent-loop-failures-2026). A tool call that comes back with its arguments retyped or its history corrupted is a transcript-handling problem, and the first thing to rule out is ordinary run-to-run variance, which is what this page measures (ollama-tool-call-history-corruption-2026).

What to assert instead: normalise, then compare, then hash

The recipe is short. Extract the tool name and the arguments, coerce a JSON-string argument into an object, compare with sorted keys, and hash the sorted form when a test needs a stable identifier. The helper below is a real file in the evidence directory, standard library only, and it is what produced the “one distinct digest” statement above when replayed over the 13 raw records:

def normalise_tool_call(message, required=None):
    calls = (message or {}).get("tool_calls") or []
    if not calls:
        return None, {}, None, ["no_tool_call"]
    fn = calls[0].get("function") or {}
    name, args, problems = fn.get("name"), fn.get("arguments"), []
    if isinstance(args, str):                 # args emitted as a JSON string
        args = json.loads(args)
    if not isinstance(args, dict):
        return name, {}, None, ["arguments_not_object"]
    problems += ["missing:" + k for k in (required or []) if k not in args]
    canon = json.dumps({"name": name, "arguments": args},
                       sort_keys=True, separators=(",", ":"))
    return name, args, hashlib.sha256(canon.encode()).hexdigest(), problems

The four cases a normaliser has to survive are the ones that actually appear in transcripts: arguments already an object; arguments emitted as a JSON string; a required argument missing; and no tool call at all. The version in normalise_tool_call.py carries those four plus the missing-argument variant as runnable self-tests, and normalise_selftest.txt is the captured output of the run, including the replay over all 13 records: one digest, five cases passing.

Normalising fixes the assertion. It does not fix the ambiguity about whether the model’s values are stable, which is why the second half of the recipe is a stability check at the settings the harness actually uses.

How to size your own check

The probe is in the evidence directory as it was run — interleaved round-robin, an internal wall-clock budget, append-only JSONL flushed before the next call starts, tolerant of str-or-dict arguments (repeat_probe.py). Point it at your own server and model, and run it in the prompt shapes your harness actually uses, not just the minimal one: in this table the flips appeared only in the two non-minimal shapes, and a stability check that only covers single-turn prompts would have reported 4/4 and 3/3 and missed them.

The decision rule is what to do with the output, and it has to respect the sample. If every call in your sample is identical, that is a statement about your sample, your model and your prompt shapes — not about determinism in general. If some calls flip, you have found the mechanism and still cannot size it from a handful of replays; report the counts with their denominators and say so. A 2/3 result is compatible with anything from a few percent to most calls flipping, and a table that prints it as “67% flaky” is inventing a rate the sample cannot support.

Every file behind the table is downloadable and was inspected for credentials and host-identifying data before publication: the raw per-call records are in run.jsonl, the one-line-per-call log including the two BUDGET_EXHAUSTED markers is probe.log, and the table above is also stored as flip_table.csv. Each record carries the condition label, the emitted tool call with its key order and both digests, and the server counters; the prompt text itself (the single-turn instruction, the history turn and the repository listing) lives in repeat_probe.py.

What this does not show

One host, one model, one fixture, 13 calls, a shared machine. Nothing here estimates a flip rate, and nothing here attributes the key-order difference to the model or to the server — the measurement scores the serialised response and stops there. Only qwen3:0.6b was run, so there is no quantisation comparison and no two-model comparison. The fixture instruction has one obviously correct call, which means argument-value drift under genuine ambiguity is untested and is a different question from the key-order drift observed here. The vendor pages establish what is promised, not what a specific server build implements, and none of them was checked for version drift against Ollama 0.20.3.

The follow-up that would change the picture is ordinary and unglamorous: the same fixture across two models, with N large enough on an idle host to separate a rate from a coincidence. Until someone runs it, the safe harness is the one that normalises before comparing — safe regardless of how these counts replicate — and the safe benchmark claim is the one that names its sample size instead of implying determinism it never measured.

Related reading: the principle that eval scores move between runs, at benchmark scale rather than at the level of one emitted call, is covered in llm-benchmark-variance-2026; the request shape and tool registry used here are in ollama-api-local-llm-integration-developer-guide-2026; what the same registry costs in prompt tokens is in ollama-tool-definition-prompt-token-cost-2026; and how to declare the assertion this table justifies is in assert-agent-evaluation-harness-2026.
